It designates the treasurer as the financial steward of a campaign finance entity, requires candidates to appoint the chair and treasurer of their candidate campaign committees, repeals the requirement that campaign managers be registered Maryland voters, and permits candidates or responsible officers to designate authorized agents to assist with campaign duties. In addition, the bill prohibits candidates from personally making disbursements from designated campaign accounts while requiring candidates to maintain knowledge of all campaign disbursements.
qa_results.stakeholders: Political candidates, campaign finance entities, campaign chairs, treasurers, campaign managers, and authorized campaign agents in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to have a direct, material impact on State finances and has no local government fiscal effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This is a departmental bill requested by the State Board of Elections. SBE is the primary agency responsible for regulating campaign finance, prescribing appointment and resignation forms, receiving entity filings, and assessing civil penalties for violations of these campaign finance requirements.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is charged with investigating and prosecuting violations of state election laws, including campaign finance violations and misuse of campaign funds. Alterations to authorized disbursements and candidate access to campaign funds are relevant to its investigative and enforcement jurisdiction.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals the requirement that an individual convicted as an adult for an offense committed as a minor must have been sentenced before October 1, 2021, to file a motion to reduce the duration of their sentence under the Juvenile Restoration Act, provided they have been imprisoned for at least 20 years.
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals convicted as adults for offenses committed as minors sentenced on or after October 1, 2021, crime victims and their representatives, State's Attorneys, and correctional authorities.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Because eligible individuals must have served at least 20 years of imprisonment, any impact on State finances, court operations, or local State's Attorneys' offices is not expected to occur within the five-year forecast period and would only materialize in future out-years.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill allows individuals convicted as adults for offenses committed as minors to file motions to reduce the duration of their sentence regardless of their sentencing date, requiring the circuit courts to receive motions, schedule and conduct hearings, and issue written decisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender represents indigent individuals in criminal and post-conviction proceedings, including filing motions and representing eligible clients at sentence modification hearings authorized under the Juvenile Restoration Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department houses incarcerated individuals who may become eligible to have their sentences reduced or be released as a result of sentence reduction motions under the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Senate Bill 163 requires the Office of the Comptroller to conduct a study and report to the Governor and General Assembly by December 1, 2026, on Maryland residents with foreign earned income under § 911 of the Internal Revenue Code, including the number of such residents, how many exceed the federal exclusion limit and by what amount, and the countries from which the income was earned.
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents earning foreign earned income subject to federal tax exclusions and the Office of the Comptroller.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State revenues are not affected. The Office of the Comptroller can conduct the study and complete the report using existing budgeted resources. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Office of the Comptroller to conduct a study on Maryland residents reporting foreign earned income under Internal Revenue Code § 911 and submit a report with its findings to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.
The bill designates the Governor as a required recipient of the Comptroller's study and report regarding foreign earned income by December 1, 2026.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Monica Cooper Prerelease Act alters the specifications, capacity requirements, site parameters, and completion timelines for establishing a comprehensive rehabilitative prerelease facility for incarcerated women in Baltimore City. It defines eligible individuals as women within 36 months of release who have prerelease or minimum security status, expands required evidence-based, trauma-informed, and gender-responsive programming (including public benefits screening and assistance), and mandates ongoing oversight and annual progress reporting by the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (DPSCS), in coordination with the Department of General Services (DGS) and oversight by the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman (OCO)
qa_results.stakeholders: Female incarcerated individuals in Maryland correctional facilities (specifically those within 36 months of release with prerelease or minimum security status) and correctional personnel.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $51,822 in FY 2027 and $86,173 in FY 2028 (rising to $98,500 by FY 2031) for the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman to hire one staff member for oversight and reporting. The bill also requires restarting planning and design for the facility on a new 3-acre Baltimore City site, which will significantly increase capital costs beyond the previous $107.8 million estimate (delaying or reducing funds for other State capital projects) and will substantially increase operating and staffing costs upon opening in FY 2032. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It must identify a site, acquire property, design, construct, and operate a comprehensive rehabilitative prerelease facility for eligible female incarcerated individuals in Baltimore City, expand trauma-informed and gender-responsive programming, and submit required progress reports.

DGS is directly mandated to assist in the planning, design, and construction of the facility. The bill requires DGS to submit a timeline of deliverables to legislative committees, manage property acquisition and procurement, and provide formal progress updates on design and construction.

qa_results.bill_summary: Mason's Law requires Maryland municipalities to inventory all publicly and privately owned existing open drainage inlets by July 1, 2027, develop a prioritization plan by April 1, 2028, to address inlets posing public safety risks, and complete safety improvements (such as approved grating systems or fencing) on prioritized inlets by April 1, 2031. It also requires all new open drainage inlets in municipalities to have approved grating systems and directs the Maryland Department of the Environment to allocate $250,000 annually in matching grants from the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program in fiscal years 2029 through 2031 to assist municipalities with installation costs.
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland municipalities, municipal residents, and private property owners with open drainage inlets
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not expected to be materially affected overall because the $250,000 required annually in FY 2029 through FY 2031 for municipal matching grants will be reallocated from existing funding within MDE's Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program. For local governments, expenditures may increase significantly beginning in FY 2027 to inventory inlets and carry out mandated improvements by April 1, 2031, partially offset by state matching grants and potential long-term maintenance savings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDE administers the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program, which is amended by the bill to require the allocation of $250,000 annually from fiscal years 2029 through 2031 to provide matching funds to municipalities for improvements to existing open drainage inlets.

SHA was analyzed extensively in the fiscal note regarding potential operational and fiscal impacts of new drainage inlet standards for state-maintained roads and drainage infrastructure located within municipal borders.
MDOT is the parent agency of the State Highway Administration and served as an information source for the fiscal analysis regarding drainage and highway maintenance within municipalities.

The bill's underlying statutory provisions require MDE to consult with the Department of Planning on regulations and coordinate clearinghouse reviews for flood control and watershed management grants.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes felony penalties of up to 10 years imprisonment for possessing, distributing, or viewing child pornography involving 100 or more images or depicting a minor under 13 years of age, and defines counting rules where each video depiction counts as 20 images.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals accused or convicted of child pornography offenses, victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation, state prosecutors, the judiciary, and state correctional facilities.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase minimally beginning in fiscal 2027 due to increased incarceration costs for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services (averaging approximately $5,838 per month per inmate). State revenues are unaffected, and local government finances and operations are not expected to be materially impacted.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new felony penalties carrying sentences of up to 10 years imprisonment for possessing, viewing, or distributing certain quantities of child pornography or depictions of children under 13, directly impacting DPSCS correctional facility intake and expenditures.
The Judiciary and circuit courts will adjudicate cases, trials, and sentencing under the newly enacted felony provisions and sentence-stacking authorizations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender will provide legal representation to indigent individuals charged with these new and enhanced felony offenses.
As the primary state law enforcement agency conducting criminal investigations, MSP is responsible for investigating child exploitation, cybercrimes, and child pornography offenses statewide.
The Office of the Attorney General represents the State in criminal appeals resulting from convictions under Maryland's child pornography statutes.

qa_results.bill_summary: Transfers the management, administration, and fund holding of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program and Fund from the Maryland Energy Administration to the Maryland Clean Energy Center. Additionally, it modifies annual reporting requirements for the Strategic Energy Investment Fund by raising the transaction reporting threshold to amounts exceeding $10,000 and requiring estimates of greenhouse gas emissions reductions instead of electricity savings.
qa_results.stakeholders: Nonprofit organizations, local jurisdictions, State agencies, and commercial businesses eligible for energy conservation loans, as well as the Maryland Energy Administration and Maryland Clean Energy Center.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has an overall net fiscal impact of $0. In FY 2027, the transfer of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund balance ($11.4 million) and ongoing revenues and expenditures results in a net special fund expenditure increase of $9.0 million and a special fund revenue decrease of $947,700 for the Maryland Energy Administration. Concurrently, nonbudgeted revenues increase by $12.3 million and nonbudgeted expenditures increase by $2.4 million for the Maryland Clean Energy Center. In future years, ongoing special fund revenues and expenditures decrease with equal corresponding increases in nonbudgeted funds. Local government finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: SB 223 directly transfers the management, supervision, administration, and holding of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program and its associated Fund to the Maryland Clean Energy Center.

The bill transfers MEA's only loan program (the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program) out of the agency and modifies MEA's statutory annual reporting requirements for the Strategic Energy Investment Fund.
The bill relieves the State Treasurer of the responsibility to hold, invest, and reinvest moneys of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund, moving those assets outside the State Treasury to MCEC.
The bill repeals the requirement that the Comptroller account for the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund as the fund is transferred out of the State Treasury to MCEC.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes that engaging in nonconsensual sexual contact with another person in connection with a first-, second-, or third-degree burglary constitutes a third-degree sexual offense. It also establishes sex offender registration requirements for this offense, classifying offenders as Tier I if the victim is an adult, Tier II if the victim is a minor at least 13 years old, and Tier III if the victim is a minor under 13 years old.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals accused or convicted of sexual offenses committed during burglaries, victims of sexual offenses, law enforcement agencies, and state correctional facilities.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures may experience a potential minimal increase due to longer periods of incarceration resulting from enhanced penalties and changes in sex offender registration classifications, though DPSCS does not anticipate a notable impact. State revenues are unaffected. Local revenues may experience a potential minimal decrease because fourth-degree sexual offenses carry a fine of up to $1,000 whereas third-degree sexual offenses carry no fine; local expenditures are unaffected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS operates the state correctional facilities where individuals convicted of third-degree felony sexual offenses serving sentences over 18 months will be incarcerated, and it oversees parole, probation, and aspects of the sex offender registry.
AOC provides operational and administrative support for the Maryland court system, including the circuit courts where these newly classified felony cases will be adjudicated.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: OPD represents indigent defendants facing criminal charges, including felony third-degree sexual offense charges created by the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill regulates the sale, transfer, or alternate use of cemeteries and abandoned cemeteries in Maryland. It prohibits registered cemeterians, permit holders, and exempt cemetery owners from selling or transferring a cemetery without the approval of the Director of the Office of Cemetery Oversight (OCO), requiring owners to submit an application, develop a preservation plan, and fulfill public notice and hearing requirements. It also grants standing to interested parties—including descendant community organizations—to bring court actions regarding proposed cemetery dispositions, and authorizes state and local governments to acquire abandoned cemeteries to transfer them to qualifying descendant, veterans, or nonprofit organizations for preservation.
qa_results.stakeholders: Cemetery owners and operators (registered cemeterians and permit holders), descendant communities and organizations, families of individuals interred in cemeteries, burial plot holders, genealogical and historical preservation organizations, and local governments.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Department of Legislative Services (DLS) advises that the Office of Cemetery Oversight and the Judiciary can implement the bill's provisions using existing budgeted resources due to the limited expected number of cemetery sales or transfers (though OCO estimated a need of $158,237 in FY 2027). The bill has no effect on State revenues and does not directly affect local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of Cemetery Oversight (OCO) is an agency within the Maryland Department of Labor. The bill tasks the Director of OCO with approving cemetery sales and transfers, reviewing applications and preservation plans, considering descendant community input, and facilitating reinterments.

The bill creates specific causes of action for parties disputing OCO decisions or seeking cemetery transfers, requiring circuit courts to conduct hearings, enter specific judgments regarding property disposition, and make determinations within six months.

The Maryland Historical Trust (housed within the Department of Planning) is involved in identifying persons in interest for burial sites under the Real Property Article referenced by the bill, and participates in statewide cemetery preservation and inventory efforts.

The bill contains an explicit statutory exemption specifying that its requirements do not apply to property acquired by the Maryland Department of Transportation that is necessary for a public project.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Modernizing Civil Relief for Service Members Act authorizes active duty service members and their spouses who relocate to Maryland under military service orders to practice their occupation or profession under a valid out-of-state license, subject to meeting certain application and good-standing requirements. It also expands eligibility for existing expedited licensing pathways by eliminating the provision that restricted 'eligible veteran' and 'eligible spouse' status to veterans discharged within one year of applying.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor, Maryland State Department of Education, Maryland Department of Health, Maryland Department of Agriculture, and various State occupational and professional licensing authorities
qa_results.stakeholders: Active duty service members, military spouses, eligible veterans, and employers seeking to hire licensed professionals relocating to Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $80,100 in FY 2027 and between $43,600 and $50,300 annually thereafter, primarily for a part-time administrative position and licensing platform updates at the Maryland State Department of Education ($67,429 in FY 2027) and IT programming updates for the Judiciary ($12,709 in FY 2027). Special fund expenditures increase by at least $27,800 in FY 2027 for software modifications at the Maryland Department of Agriculture ($15,000) and the Maryland Department of Labor ($12,792), with potential additional system costs for health occupations boards. State general and special fund revenues decrease by an indeterminate amount beginning in FY 2027 due to reduced occupational and professional licensing fee collections. Local revenues from certain business licenses may also experience minimal decreases.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends licensing requirements across numerous occupational and professional boards under MD Labor, including accountancy, architecture, barbers, cosmetologists, electricians, engineers, real estate, and financial regulation, and requires IT updates to licensing systems.

The bill amends practice requirements and expedited licensing provisions across more than twenty health occupations boards housed within MDH, as well as MDH permits for medical laboratories and tissue banks.

MSDE is directly responsible for expedited educator licensure and teacher certifications affected by the bill; the fiscal note projects increased general fund expenditures for a new staff position and teacher licensure system programming.

The bill exempts qualifying active duty service members and spouses from state licensing for veterinary medicine, pesticide application, nutrient management, and fertilizer application, resulting in anticipated software update costs and licensing fee reductions.

MDE and its affiliated boards oversee several environmental licenses and certifications affected by the bill, including scrap tire handling/recycling, well drilling, on-site wastewater, waterworks operations, and marine contracting.

MVA issues and regulates vehicle salesmen, automotive dismantlers and recyclers, title service agents, driving schools, and driving instructors, all of which are subject to the bill's out-of-state license recognition.
MDOT oversees the Motor Vehicle Administration, whose professional and commercial vehicle-related licenses are directly amended by the bill.

The Secretary of State Police licenses private detectives, security guards, and security systems technicians, while MSP's Automotive Safety Enforcement Division licenses vehicle inspection mechanics and the State Fire Marshal certifies nongovernmental electrical inspectors and explosives handlers.

Circuit court clerks issue several business licenses affected by the bill (traders, peddlers, and junk dealers), bar admission provisions are amended, and the Judiciary incurs programming costs for elicensing system updates.
The PSC's licensing requirements for energy salespersons, energy vendors, and master plumber/gasfitters are amended to accommodate qualifying service members and spouses.
The bill amends licensing statutes enforced by the Insurance Commissioner for insurance producers, advisers, bail bondsmen, public adjusters, and motor club services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency's licensing requirements for video lottery operation/employment and sports wagering operations are amended under the bill.
DNR licenses commercial taxidermists and tree experts, both of which are amended by the bill to recognize out-of-state credentials for active service members and spouses.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS and the EMS Board license emergency medical services providers, whose licensing mandates under the Education Article are modified by the bill.
The Commission registers and regulates rehabilitation counselors, vocational evaluators, and case managers under Labor and Employment § 9-6A-09, which is amended by the bill.
The Comptroller issues transient vendor licenses amended by the bill and administers tire recycling fee collections and remittances.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services licenses private home detention monitoring agencies, which are amended under the bill.

As the primary agency advocating for and assisting Maryland's active service members, veterans, and military families, DVMF is directly interested in the modernizing civil relief and occupational license portability provisions.

The bill updates SCRA provisions regarding contract terminations for service members relocating on orders and explicitly requires service providers to give notice of rights posted on the Maryland National Guard's website.

qa_results.bill_summary: Enacts the Voting Rights Act of 2026 for counties and municipal corporations, prohibiting local government election methods that impair or dilute the voting strength of protected classes (defined by race, color, or language minority groups). The bill authorizes the Office of the Attorney General or private individuals to file legal actions to challenge discriminatory election systems, outlines criteria for proving polarized voting and violations, and empowers courts to order tailored remedies and award attorney's fees.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
qa_results.stakeholders: Voters belonging to racial, color, or language minority protected classes, candidates for local office, and county and municipal governments and their governing bodies.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase to the extent the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) enforces the bill's provisions. OAG estimated an increase of $242,704 in FY 2027 for one Assistant Attorney General and expert witness costs, though the Department of Legislative Services notes actual enforcement costs depend on the level of private versus state litigation. State revenues are unaffected, and local government finances are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Office of the Attorney General to bring civil enforcement actions against counties and municipal corporations for violations of the Voting Rights Act of 2026, which may require additional staffing and litigation expenditures as noted in the fiscal note.

The bill establishes causes of action, legal standards, evidentiary criteria, preliminary relief procedures, and remedial powers for Maryland courts hearing claims regarding local voting rights violations.

The Maryland State Board of Elections oversees election administration across the state and the 24 local boards of elections, which may be impacted by court-ordered remedies or alterations to election methods in county and municipal jurisdictions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes special enforcement officers in Baltimore City to inspect retailers and enforce laws regulating cigarettes, other tobacco products, and electronic smoking devices, while allowing the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission to penalize violators. It requires retailers in Baltimore City to obtain a local licensure authorization from the Mayor and City Council before receiving or renewing a county license, imposes a one-year moratorium on new retail licenses from October 1, 2026, to October 1, 2027, and directs 50% of authorization request fees to the Family League of Baltimore City, Inc.
qa_results.stakeholders: Tobacco and electronic smoking device retailers in Baltimore City, the Baltimore City Health Department, the Family League of Baltimore City, Inc., and consumers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues and expenditures increase by an indeterminate amount as 50% of local licensure authorization fees are remitted to the Comptroller and distributed to the Family League of Baltimore City, Inc. State general fund revenues also increase by an indeterminate amount assuming the remaining 50% is remitted to ATCC, alongside a minimal one-time general fund expenditure increase for Judiciary programming in FY 2027. Baltimore City expenditures increase by an indeterminate amount for local enforcement and administering authorizations; city revenues are not expected to be affected as fee proceeds are remitted to the State.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Comptroller with receiving 50% of the licensure authorization request fees collected by Baltimore City and distributing those funds to the Family League of Baltimore City, Inc. in a specified manner.

Clerks of the Circuit Court (supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts) issue retail county tobacco and electronic smoking device licenses and must verify licensure authorization from Baltimore City before issuance; the Judiciary incurs one-time programming expenses to implement these changes.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Budget Bill for Fiscal Year 2027 makes appropriations for the support of State government, payments to civil divisions, operating and capital expenses across executive departments, the General Assembly, the Judiciary, and various State institutions, as well as providing deficiency appropriations for Fiscal Year 2026.
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland State agencies, local governments, public school students and educators, healthcare providers, state employees, public transit riders, and Maryland residents receiving state services and benefits.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes total appropriations across all funds for Fiscal Year 2027 of approximately $70.84 billion (reflecting $70.94 billion in gross appropriations less $100.0 million in estimated agency general fund reversions), along with supplemental and FY 2026 deficiency appropriations. It funds state governmental operations, debt service, K-12 education formulas, Medicaid, higher education institutions, and local aid distributions.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loan of 2026 authorizes the issuance of general obligation bonds to fund capital improvements across Maryland, including public school construction, higher education facilities, healthcare and community facilities, parks and environmental projects, and local community grants. The act also deauthorizes certain prior bond loan allocations, preauthorizes bond debt for future fiscal years, and amends statutory provisions governing capital appropriations, matching requirements, and termination timelines.
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland local governments, public school systems, state universities and community colleges, health and human service facilities, nonprofit grant recipients, and Maryland taxpayers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: Authorizes $1,847,099,000 in State general obligation debt, offset by $97,099,000 in deauthorizations of previously approved bond debt, yielding $1,750,000,000 in net new authorized debt, along with $5,000,000 in bond premium authorizations. Debt service will be funded through the statewide property tax over a 15-year repayment period. The bill also preauthorizes $511,006,000 for FY 2028, $230,424,000 for FY 2029, and $36,349,000 for FY 2030. Local effect: Local jurisdictions benefit from hundreds of millions in grant allocations for public school construction, parks, infrastructure, community centers, and local public initiatives, with certain matching fund requirements waived or amended.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Board of Public Works is the primary authority responsible for borrowing money and issuing State general obligation bonds, approving capital expenditures, certifying matching funds, and approving grant allocations and contract awards under the Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loan.

DBM exercises central fiscal oversight over the capital program, including reviewing project programs and outline plans, approving fund reallocations between design and construction, and administering the Construction Contingency Fund.

DGS oversees state facility construction, corrects technical grant documentation under Section 1(9)(b), and is assigned a new statutory annual reporting requirement to the General Assembly regarding unencumbered miscellaneous capital grants.
DHCD receives tens of millions of dollars in capital bond authorizations across numerous community development, neighborhood revitalization, and affordable housing loan and grant programs.

MDE receives substantial capital appropriations to fund environmental infrastructure, including the Bay Restoration Fund, Water Quality and Drinking Water Revolving Loan Funds, and flood management programs.

The IAC is a primary implementing body that administers hundreds of millions of dollars authorized for the Public School Construction Program, the Nancy K. Kopp Priority Fund, nonpublic aging schools, and supplemental school grants.
The Treasurer receives bond sale proceeds, manages bond issuances, determines premium transfers to the Annuity Bond Fund, and submits annual debt termination reports.
The Comptroller credits bond proceeds and bond premiums on the State's books, disburses capital expenditures upon BPW approval, and assists in debt reconciliation reporting.
USM receives substantial direct capital bond allocations for academic buildings, health centers, research facilities, and infrastructure improvements across multiple member campuses.
MSDE co-administers capital grants with the IAC, including the Nonpublic Aging Schools Program and allocations for local school facility improvements.
DNR receives direct capital appropriations for Community Parks and Playgrounds, the Natural Resources Development Fund, Waterway Improvement projects, and the Oyster Restoration Program.
MDH receives capital funding for the Clifton T. Perkins Hospital Center renovation, the Community Health Facilities Grant Program, and Federally Qualified Health Centers grants.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS receives capital authorizations for perimeter fence and security replacements at correctional facilities (MCI-H and RCI) and sees modifications to pre-release facility funding.
MDOT receives major capital authorizations for Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) capital upgrades ($167M) as well as capital improvements impacting transit-oriented sites.
MDA receives $8M for the Maryland Agricultural Cost-Share Program and manages capital modifications for the Salisbury Animal Health Laboratory.
DJS receives $4.29M to begin design of the New Cheltenham Youth Treatment Center and has prior capital appropriations modified for female detention and educational facilities.

MDP (through the Maryland Historical Trust) receives $5M for the African American Heritage Preservation Program, $1M+ for Historic Preservation Grants, and is mandated to receive historic preservation easements on funded grant projects.
The Military Department receives capital appropriations for vehicle maintenance shops, readiness centers, and related facility infrastructure in Hagerstown, Frederick, and Camp Fretterd.
MES receives millions from the State Water and Sewer Infrastructure Improvement Fund to design and construct utility and wastewater upgrades across state institutions.
Morgan State receives major multi-year capital funding for campus-wide electrical infrastructure upgrades and Phase II of its New Science Center.
MSD receives substantial capital appropriations and multi-year preauthorizations for constructing new student residences and support facilities on its Frederick campus.
MHEC administers the Community College Construction Grant Program and the Community College Facilities Renewal Grant Program funded extensively in the bill.
MHEC administers the Community College Construction Grant Program ($56.7M+ in FY 2027 plus preauthorizations) and the Facilities Renewal Grant Program.
Commerce administers the Maryland Arts Capital Grant Program, which receives $3M in bond authorizations for arts facility and infrastructure improvements.
The department receives $1.124M for the Access Maryland program to finance architectural modifications and improve accessibility in State-owned facilities.
DoIT receives $16.268M to continue equipment installation and construction of the Maryland FiRST Public Safety Radio System.
MSP receives capital bond funding for design and construction projects at Barrack A (Waterloo), Barrack J (Annapolis), and Barrack L (Forestville).
The bill embodies the executive capital budget, requires executive decisions regarding unspent bond proceeds under SFP 8-129, and finances key administration priorities.
The bill funds major Judicial Branch capital projects, including construction of the new Supreme Court of Maryland Building and the Washington County District Court.
The agency administers the Public Library Capital Grant Program funded at $12.775M and has prior authorizations adjusted for the State Library Resource Center.
The commission receives capital bond funding for site infrastructure improvements and visitor center conversions, as well as an extension on prior interpretive center funds.
St. Mary's College receives direct capital funding for campus infrastructure improvements and renovations to Montgomery Hall.
The bill amends prior capital authorizations to extend the termination date for grants awarded under MDoA's Senior Centers Capital Grant Program.

MEDCO receives multiple direct capital grants, including $7.5M for low iron quartz/calcined clay facilities, $1M for sensitive compartmented information facilities, and $5M for North Locust Point Terminal improvements.
TEDCO receives a $2M grant to support capital projects in regenerative medicine and advanced manufacturing.
MPA is identified to coordinate with MEDCO on a $5M capital grant project for infrastructure improvements to the North Locust Point Terminal.
SHA is designated to coordinate with Montgomery County on a grant-funded safety improvements project on Route 198.
The bill includes capital funding for infrastructure at the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home and references matching funds for a new State Veterans Home in Sykesville.
The bill alters a prior bond authorization amount for the expansion and renovation of Studio A at Maryland Public Television.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2026 alters mandated appropriations, authorizes transfers from various special funds to the General Fund, adjusts funding formulas for community colleges and higher education institutions, decouples Maryland tax code from certain federal bonus and production property depreciation provisions, increases local government contributions toward teacher retirement costs, and enacts diverse cost-containment and administrative measures to balance the State budget.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Budget and Management and the Comptroller of Maryland
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland taxpayers, businesses, local governments and school systems, community colleges, public and private four-year higher education institutions, state employees, teachers, healthcare providers, and program beneficiaries.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State General Fund revenues increase by $808.0 million in FY 2026 and $218.9 million in FY 2027, while General Fund expenditures decrease by $2.1 million in FY 2026 and $651.2 million in FY 2027 (totaling a $1.68 billion General Fund budget improvement across FY 2026 and FY 2027). Special fund revenues decrease by $3.9 million in FY 2026 and $405.5 million in FY 2027; special fund expenditures increase by $61.2 million in FY 2026 and decrease by $111.0 million in FY 2027. Local finances are significantly affected beginning in FY 2027: county expenditures increase by $39.3 million annually due to a shift in teacher pension costs, while direct State aid for community colleges is reduced by $21.0 million in FY 2027, partially offset by an estimated $29.9 million in local revenue gains from federal tax decoupling modifications.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DBM is the state's principal fiscal agency and is directly tasked with determining noncompliance disputes regarding local immigration enforcement agreements, processing budget amendments for the Population Health Improvement Fund, consulting on expedited procurements for the Developmental Disabilities Administration, and managing the overall state budget adjustments.

The Comptroller is responsible for implementing numerous major tax and revenue provisions, including decoupling from federal bonus and production property depreciation deductions, pass-through entity tax modifications and reporting, setting refund interest rates on the digital advertising tax, executing large fund transfers (including $380 million from the Local Income Tax Reserve Account), and suspending police aid distributions to noncompliant local entities.

MDH is heavily impacted by provisions altering county reimbursement schedules for Assisted Outpatient Treatment (AOT) programs, removing statutory retention period mandates for the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, funding Medicaid through the Population Health Improvement Fund and Cigarette Restitution Fund, utilizing health occupation board fund balances, and authorizing expedited procurement for the Developmental Disabilities Administration.

MHEC is directly responsible for administering adjusted funding formulas and statutory reductions, including the Senator John A. Cade Formula cap for community colleges, freezing the Joseph A. Sellinger formula funding, altering caps and reporting dates for the Student Loan Debt Relief Tax Credit, and managing reductions to the Police Officers and Probation Agents scholarship and loan repayment programs.

MEA administers the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which is subjected to substantial fund transfers ($259 million from the RPS/ACP account and $33 million from the Administration account) and statutory expansions of allowable uses for clean energy, grid research, and climate initiatives.

MSDE is impacted by the temporary cap on Tier II full-day prekindergarten eligibility (limited to 450% FPL in FY 2027), the shift of $36.2 million in local school teacher pension costs to county governments, repealing the Lacrosse Opportunities Program funding mandate, and provider rate freezes through the Interagency Rates Committee.

DNR experiences a $7 million fund transfer from the Waterway Improvement Fund (to be replaced with general obligation bonds), changes to the Program Open Space land acquisition balance and fund transfers, and receives SEIF funding for power plant research and environmental review programs.

MDE is subject to a $70 million fund transfer from the Bay Restoration Fund to the General Fund (replaced by general obligation bonds) and receives SEIF funding for the Comprehensive Flood Management Grant Program and climate personnel.

MD Labor is impacted by mandate reductions for the Public Safety Apprenticeship Program and Career Pathways for Health Care Workers Program, transfers from the Non-Depository Special Fund ($3.5M) and Banking Institution Fund ($1.5M), and the requirement to reimburse $37.3 million to the Local Income Tax Reserve Account from the FAMLI Fund.

Commerce administers the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund (which is expanded to fund operating costs of DoSEM) and the More Jobs for Marylanders Program, which has its FY 2027 final tax credit certificates capped at $15 million and reserve funds transferred.
MIA is directed to order health insurance carriers maintaining segregated accounts under ACA § 1303 to transfer excess balances to the Dedicated Purpose Account for health care access grants.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is tasked with identifying and notifying local jurisdictions noncompliant with state immigration enforcement agreement laws to suspend State Aid for Police Protection funding, experiences a $2.0 million transfer from the Performance Incentive Grant Fund, and sees several DPA grant balances transferred.

MSA's required lottery distribution for the Racing and Community Development Financing Fund is reduced from $17.0 million to $13.4 million in FY 2026, and its FY 2027 lottery distribution for the Blue Line Corridor Facility Fund is redirected to specific localized economic development grants.

MDOT receives $10 million from SEIF ACP revenues to create right-of-way leasing and safety guidelines for transmission infrastructure and experiences special fund revenue impacts in the Transportation Trust Fund from corporate tax decoupling and historic vehicle registrations.
MVA must implement the change in eligibility criteria for Class L historic motor vehicle registrations from model year 1999 or earlier to vehicles at least 25 years old starting in FY 2028.

HSCRC is required to study and examine hospital rate adjustments of up to $140 million to provide financial assistance to Medicare Advantage plans and coordinates uses of the Population Health Improvement Fund.
MDA is impacted by reductions to statutory funding mandates for the Maryland Healthy Soils Program and the Urban Agriculture Water and Power Infrastructure Grant Fund.

DJS is authorized to repurpose a $3.0 million FY 2026 appropriation to reopen the Alfred D. Noyes Children's Center as a facility for children and provide drug treatment across other facilities, and is subject to provider rate restrictions under the Interagency Rates Committee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DSCI's statutory participation targets for the Maryland Corps Young Adult Service Year Option Pathway are reduced for FY 2027 and FY 2028, resulting in general fund expenditure reductions.

The bill represents the Administration's Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2026, implementing the Governor's proposed budget adjustments, statutory mandate relief, and fund balance transfer authorizations.
BPW receives SEIF funding for the Chesapeake Conservation and Climate Corps Program and oversees expedited procurement requests for DDA data analytics contracts.
MDEM receives SEIF funding to support agency resiliency initiatives and the annual report of the Office of Resilience.
DGS receives a $20 million special fund appropriation from SEIF ACP revenues in FY 2027 for renewable energy and solar development on state property.
DHCD receives SEIF funding to support two positions within its Housing and Building Energy program.
DHS is subject to the provider rate freeze under the Interagency Rates Committee for residential child care facilities and previously utilized emergency Fiscal Responsibility Fund allocations.

DoIT's Information Technology Investment Fund receives a $59.3 million special fund appropriation in FY 2026 from the Fiscal Responsibility Fund to support Major Information Technology Development Projects (MITDPs).

MDP receives SEIF funding for a Lead Resilience Planner and administers the African American Heritage Preservation Program, which is authorized to award noncapital grants if funding exceeds the capital mandate.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is impacted by a $2.0 million transfer from the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission Fund to the General Fund.
IAC is authorized to reallocate $40 million in expiring federal ARPA State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds from prior years for school HVAC upgrades to ensure federal compliance.
MEDCO is designated to receive an $18 million grant from redirected lottery revenues for a mixed-use development and soccer stadium project at the University of Maryland, College Park.
MHBE receives a $250,000 transfer from the Child Care Capital Support Revolving Loan Fund to conduct an outreach and health insurance survey among child care providers.
MSA provides staff support for the Maryland Reparations Commission, which has its membership expanded, reporting dates extended, and termination date extended through FY 2029.
MSLA's budget includes an altered local employer share of retirement contributions for librarians, shifting $722,970 annually to local governments.

The Maryland State Police Aviation Command's general operating expenses are authorized to be supported by $5.5 million annually from the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund (MEMSOF) through FY 2029.
SRA receives and manages the restructured $39.3 million annual local employer pension contributions for local school systems, community colleges, and library staff shifted from the State to counties.
PSC is allocated $10 million from SEIF compliance fee revenues in FY 2027 to conduct research into grid-enhancing and advanced transmission technologies.
USM institutions are affected by formulas calculating higher education aid, research grant allocations within the Dedicated Purpose Account, and a planned soccer stadium project at UMCP.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is referenced in connection with partnerships under the Cannabis Business Assistance Fund, though operating expenses are redirected to DoSEM.

The State Treasurer manages investments for special funds such as the More Jobs for Marylanders Tax Credit Reserve Fund and oversees general fund cash management impacted by the bill's large fund transfers.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits a court or a party in a criminal or juvenile delinquency case from disclosing or permitting inspection of case filings or records to nonparties unless identifying information of victims of sexual assault or stalking is redacted, with exceptions for good cause. It also requires courts to redact such information upon written request from the victim and creates a petition process for health occupations boards to access unredacted filings to investigate sexual misconduct allegations.
qa_results.stakeholders: Victims of sexual assault and stalking, defendants, parties and nonparties in criminal and juvenile cases, State's Attorneys, and health occupations boards
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Judiciary increase by $13,500 in FY 2027 for one-time computer programming costs. The bill is not expected to materially affect local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the judicial system by requiring courts to redact identifying information of sexual assault and stalking victims from court records and filings upon notice or written request. The Administrative Office of the Courts incurs a direct fiscal impact of $13,500 in FY 2027 for necessary IT programming and case management updates.

The Maryland Department of Health houses and oversees the state health occupations licensing boards, which are explicitly authorized under the bill to petition courts for unredacted filings and records to investigate and discipline licensed professionals for sexual misconduct.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As primary defense counsel and a party in criminal and juvenile delinquency cases across Maryland, the Office of the Public Defender is directly subject to the bill's restrictions on disclosing unredacted court filings and records containing victim identifying information.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill extends by one year, through fiscal year 2029, the authorization for the Governor to include a discretionary $1.0 million appropriation in the annual state budget for operating grants to qualifying nonprofit organizations that provide automotive repair training and reentry services to incarcerated and formerly incarcerated individuals.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
qa_results.stakeholders: Incarcerated and formerly incarcerated individuals participating in reentry and automotive repair job training programs, as well as qualifying nonprofit organizations providing these services.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by an estimated $1,000,000 in FY 2029 assuming discretionary grant funds are appropriated. State revenues are unaffected, and there is no local fiscal impact. The Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy can implement and administer the grants using existing staff.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly designates the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy to administer the grant funds and receive annual expenditure and performance reports from qualifying nonprofit grantees through the extended fiscal year 2029.
The bill extends discretionary statutory authority to the Governor to include an annual appropriation of $1.0 million in the state budget bill for the operating grants through fiscal year 2029.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for preparing and supervising the annual state operating budget, which may incorporate the authorized $1.0 million general fund appropriation in fiscal year 2029.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill makes several revisions to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. Key changes include extending through fiscal 2028 the current calculation method for compensatory education enrollment; removing the sunset date on the use of Concentration of Poverty Grant funds for certain required programs like fine arts; modifying teacher certification pathways to recognize state-approved portfolios and apprenticeships; postponing the National Board Certification requirement for new principals until July 1, 2034; extending the state's authority to limit dual enrollment courses through fiscal 2030; restructuring the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee while repealing its advisory committee; suspending the Expert Review Team Program for the 2026–2027 school year; and directing the Accountability and Implementation Board and the Maryland State Department of Education to study and recommend methodologies for counting low-income students.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) and the Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB)
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland public school students (particularly low-income and CTE students), public school teachers, school administrators and prospective principals, local school systems, county governments, and postsecondary education institutions.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase by $228.5 million in FY 2027, $311.5 million in FY 2028, $170.4 million in FY 2029, $75.5 million in FY 2030, and $23.7 million in FY 2031, driven primarily by formula aid changes for compensatory education and Concentration of Poverty Grants. Blueprint special fund revenues decrease by $4.7 million in FY 2027 and $3.0 million in FY 2028 due to lower interest earnings on fund balances. At the local level, revenues and required county appropriations increase significantly in several jurisdictions, with county appropriations increasing by an estimated $6.8 million in FY 2027 and $14.5 million in FY 2028.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE is a primary implementing agency for the bill's provisions, which modify the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. MSDE is tasked with modifying teacher certification requirements, suspending the Expert Review Team Program, administering grant funding adjustments (including Concentration of Poverty Grants, the Judith P. Hoyer Program, and the Academic Excellence Fund), and collaborating to develop a methodology for counting low-income students.

The Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee is housed as a unit within GWDB. GWDB is required to collaborate on, approve, and adopt the priority occupations list and career pathway information developed by the CTE Committee.

The Secretary of Labor serves on the CTE Committee, which is staffed by MD Labor. Additionally, the department's Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning oversees registered apprenticeship pathways incorporated into post-CCR CTE standards.

The Secretary of Higher Education serves on the CTE Committee, which makes recommendations to MHEC. Additionally, the fiscal note identifies an increase in general fund expenditures for MHEC to hire an education policy analyst to align postsecondary programs with the new priority occupations list.

The Secretary of Higher Education is a member of the CTE Committee, and the commission receives recommendations on aligning postsecondary CTE systems and priority occupations, resulting in noted fiscal impacts for additional agency staffing.

The bill explicitly requires the Accountability and Implementation Board and MSDE to consult with DBM in developing a new methodology for counting low-income students for compensatory education formula funding. The bill also has major budgetary impacts on state general and special fund expenditures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill restructures the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee, alters its duties and membership composition, and formally repeals the CTE Skills Standards Advisory Committee.
The Secretary of Commerce is designated by statute as an ex officio member of the CTE Committee to ensure career technical education alignment with state economic development goals.

The Governor jointly appoints employer and industry members and the chair of the CTE Committee, and receives required reports on low-income student counting methodologies and the Expert Review Team Program.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill modifies the disqualification criteria for jury service regarding criminal convictions. It allows individuals previously convicted of a crime punishable by more than one year of imprisonment to serve on a jury once they have completed their sentence, parole, and probation. It also establishes disqualifications for individuals convicted of perjury, witness intimidation, jury intimidation, or fraud and related offenses under Title 8 of the Criminal Law Article, and repeals the provision specifically regarding pardoned individuals.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts)
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals with past criminal convictions, prospective jurors, and the Maryland court system.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $28,100 in FY 2027 only for one-time programming costs incurred by the Judiciary to update online and printed juror qualification forms. Revenues are not affected, and there is no material impact on local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters statutory disqualification standards for jury service, directly impacting court administration and requiring the Administrative Office of the Courts to expend funds to update both online and printed juror qualification forms.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Youth Charging Reform Act expands the juvenile court's jurisdiction by repealing provisions that automatically placed youth charged with certain offenses—such as first-degree assault and specific firearm violations—into adult criminal court. It mandates that juvenile intake officers authorize pre-hearing detention for youth aged 16 and older accused of handgun offenses or crimes of violence. The bill also establishes reporting requirements and, effective October 1, 2029, prohibits housing or transporting juveniles within sight or sound of incarcerated adults or confining them in adult correctional facilities, except for temporary processing of up to six hours.
qa_results.stakeholders: Juveniles charged with delinquent acts or crimes, the Department of Juvenile Services, local adult detention centers, State's Attorneys' offices, the Office of the Public Defender, and law enforcement agencies.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Effect: Department of Juvenile Services (DJS) may realize significant general fund cost savings beginning in FY 2027 due to shorter pre-disposition lengths of stay; Office of the Public Defender and Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services may also see slight expenditure decreases. Compliance with federal sight-and-sound separation mandates helps the State avoid an estimated $173,000 loss in annual federal JJDPA grant funding and the restricted reallocation of $347,000 annually beginning in FY 2030. If DJS cannot accommodate youth with existing beds, capital construction costs could arise. Local Effect: Expenditures for State's Attorneys' offices may increase significantly beginning in FY 2027 due to higher juvenile caseload workloads, while local detention facility expenditures are expected to decrease as juveniles are removed from adult jails.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts DJS by expanding juvenile court jurisdiction over certain youth offenses, requiring intake officers to authorize pre-hearing detention for specified offenses, establishing sight and sound separation standards, and mandating recurring annual reporting on detention length of stay and jurisdiction waivers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is required to submit annual reports on youth housed with adult offenders and federal Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention Act (JJDPA) violations. Additionally, GOCPP administers Title II formula grants, which are protected from federal penalties and reductions through compliance with this bill.

AOC is affected by shifts in original jurisdiction between adult criminal courts and juvenile courts, procedural changes regarding transfers and pre-hearing detention, and is required to consult with DJS on an annual report regarding juvenile waiver and transfer petitions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill restricts confining juveniles in adult facilities and requires strict sight and sound separation from incarcerated adults, impacting DPSCS correctional facilities and potentially reducing the number of youth housed or sentenced in DPSCS custody.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: OPD may see a reduction in expenditures for contractual developmental and psychological evaluations as fewer youth cases will originate in the adult criminal court system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Commission on Juvenile Justice Reform and Emerging and Best Practices receives statutory reports from DJS and GOCPP and is specifically required to submit a comprehensive implementation, incident, and staffing report to the General Assembly by October 1, 2027.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a direct admission program at participating Maryland public senior higher education institutions for eligible high school students starting in the 2028–2029 academic year. The Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC), the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), and public four-year institutions must establish eligibility requirements through a memorandum of understanding, waive application fees for direct admission applicants, and conduct an implementation and feasibility study due by July 1, 2027.
qa_results.stakeholders: Eligible Maryland high school students, public senior higher education institutions (University System of Maryland, Morgan State University, St. Mary's College of Maryland), and Maryland public high schools
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by an estimated $100,000 in FY 2027 for MHEC and MSDE to retain consultants for the required study and report. Program implementation beginning in FY 2028 for the 2028–2029 academic year will result in further, potentially significant general fund expenditures (possibly in the millions of dollars) for IT modifications, data integration, and administrative operations. Optional participation by public colleges and universities could affect institutional revenues and administrative costs depending on student enrollment outcomes. Local school systems are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is primary implementing agency tasked with administering the direct admission program, entering into an MOU for eligibility standards, establishing a conditional admission process, and conducting a feasibility and implementation study with a final report due to the General Assembly by July 1, 2027.

MHEC is the primary regulatory and coordinating board tasked with establishing direct admission eligibility requirements, administering the admissions process, and conducting the required implementation study and report.

MSDE is required to collaborate with MHEC on the direct admission study, enter into the MOU to set eligibility requirements based on college and career readiness standards, and establish the process for transmitting student eligibility data.

USM is required to collaborate with MHEC and MSDE to establish baseline eligibility requirements and sign an MOU, and its constituent institutions may choose to participate in offering direct admission to eligible students.

Morgan State University is explicitly mandated to collaborate on eligibility requirements and enter into the MOU, and may participate in the direct admission program by offering conditional direct admission.

St. Mary's College of Maryland is required to participate in developing program eligibility criteria and executing the MOU, and has the option to participate as an institution offering direct admissions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Senate Bill 334 prohibits a person from manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, purchasing, receiving, or transferring a machine gun convertible pistol beginning January 1, 2027, subject to specified exceptions such as transfers between immediate family members and law enforcement exemptions. It expands the definition of a rapid fire activator to include a pistol converter, applies existing misdemeanor penalties to violations, and requires the Department of State Police to adopt regulations and publish a list of prohibited machine gun convertible pistols.
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed firearms dealers, gunsmiths, firearm manufacturers, handgun owners and purchasers, and law enforcement agencies.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $220,200 in FY 2027, increasing annually to $262,900 by FY 2031, to fund two positions (one trooper and one civilian administrative officer) within the Department of State Police to review handguns and maintain the prohibited firearm list. State and local revenues and expenditures may experience minimal increases from expanded criminal penalty provisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates that the Department of State Police adopt regulations to implement the law, evaluate firearms on the handgun roster, and publish and maintain a list of prohibited machine gun convertible pistols, requiring additional personnel and funding.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill expands criminal offenses related to machine gun convertible pistols and pistol converters, subjecting violators to misdemeanor penalties of up to 3 years imprisonment or mandatory minimum felony sentences if used in crimes of violence, impacting state correctional facilities and supervision.
The Maryland judiciary will handle court proceedings, filings, and adjudications for criminal cases brought under the newly expanded firearm prohibitions and penalties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency will be required to provide legal defense and representation to indigent individuals charged under the bill's expanded criminal firearm prohibitions.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill authorizes vehicle dealer associations and vehicle manufacturer associations to request an administrative hearing with the Motor Vehicle Administration on behalf of themselves or their members to resolve statutory disputes or seek clarification of vehicle franchise and dealer laws, subject to specific conditions.
qa_results.stakeholders: Vehicle dealers, vehicle manufacturers, dealer and manufacturer associations, and vehicle distributors and factory branches
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local operations or finances. Any potential increase in administrative hearing caseloads for the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Office of Administrative Hearings, and the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel County can be handled with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration is the primary regulatory agency overseeing vehicle dealers, manufacturers, and distributors, and it administers the dispute resolution and hearing process under Title 12 and Title 15 of the Transportation Article.

The Maryland Department of Transportation is the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration and oversees the administration and implementation of Maryland's vehicle and transportation laws.

The Office of Administrative Hearings presides over contested cases and administrative hearings requested through the Motor Vehicle Administration regarding disputes between dealers, manufacturers, and their associations.
Decisions and orders resulting from administrative hearings held under this subtitle may be appealed to the Circuit Court system, which is supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

qa_results.bill_summary: The bill establishes the 'No Kings Act,' authorizing an aggrieved party or the Maryland Office of the Attorney General to bring a civil action against a 'covered officer' (such as a federal law enforcement officer authorized to carry firearms and make arrests for U.S. Code violations) who, under color of law, deprives the party of rights secured under the U.S. Constitution or federal law. It allows courts to grant damages, declaratory and injunctive relief, and award reasonable attorney's and expert witness fees to prevailing plaintiffs, subject to a five-year statute of limitations.
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals alleging deprivation of constitutional or federal rights, covered federal law enforcement officers, the Office of the Attorney General, the state judicial system, and civil rights litigation attorneys.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to affect State liability or materially impact State expenditures. General fund revenues may increase to the extent the Office of the Attorney General is awarded damages or recovers reasonable fees and costs in lawsuits brought under the bill. Local government finances and operations are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Office of the Attorney General to initiate civil actions against covered officers who deprive individuals of federal constitutional or statutory rights, and allows the office to seek damages, declaratory/injunctive relief, and attorney's fees.

The State Treasurer's Office manages state liability and tort claims under the Maryland Tort Claims Act (MTCA); the agency evaluated the bill's potential impact on sovereign immunity and anticipated potential caseload and claim adjustments arising from federal-state law enforcement actions.

The bill establishes a new statutory civil cause of action within the Maryland Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article, directly impacting court filings, judicial proceedings, and court administration.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill renames the Young Readers Matching Grant Program to the Young Readers Grant Program, removes matching fund requirements, increases its mandated annual appropriation from $350,000 to $450,000, adjusts public library service requirements, and increases the per capita State aid funding formulas for regional resource centers and county public library systems beginning in fiscal year 2028 through fiscal year 2032 and beyond.
qa_results.stakeholders: County public library systems, regional resource centers, young readers and children in low-income areas, and Maryland library patrons.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $1.3 million in FY 2028, rising to $5.2 million in FY 2031 due to higher per capita funding mandates for regional resource centers and local library systems, alongside a $100,000 annual increase for the Young Readers Grant Program. State aid to local library systems increases by $1.2 million in FY 2028 and $5.1 million in FY 2031. Local expenditures are not expected to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs programs administered by the Maryland State Library Agency, specifically renaming and altering the Young Readers Grant Program administered by the State Librarian and State Library Board, while also updating the funding formulas and service requirements for regional resource centers and county public library systems.

DBM is responsible for state budget preparation and supervision, and the bill increases mandated general fund appropriations for the Young Readers Grant Program and per capita aid formulas for regional resource centers and local libraries beginning in fiscal 2028.
The bill mandates that the Governor include an increased annual appropriation of $450,000 in the state budget bill for the Young Readers Grant Program.

The bill outlines a statutory enforcement role for the Comptroller to withhold state aid funds from any county library system certified by the State Library Board as failing to meet state library operating standards.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill increases the compensation range for the full-time chief inspector employed by the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners by altering the position's pay grade from non-represented pay schedule NR-05 to NR-12.
qa_results.responsible_party: Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: The full-time chief inspector and the Anne Arundel County Board of License Commissioners.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: The bill is not expected to materially affect Anne Arundel County finances or operations. While the bill shifts the pay scale from NR-05 ($36,378 to $67,252 in FY 2026) to NR-12 ($51,405 to $95,034 in FY 2026), it does not directly mandate an immediate salary increase or decrease, and the board funds operations through licensing fees.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill codifies and sets requirements for the Community Forensic Aftercare Program (CFAP) within the Maryland Department of Health to monitor individuals committed as not criminally responsible who are on conditional release, as well as certain individuals found incompetent to stand trial. It establishes a community monitoring board to make decisions and recommendations on conditional release and travel requests, prohibits CFAP from making clinical treatment decisions, and updates rules for facility forensic review boards regarding notice and virtual agent attendance.
qa_results.stakeholders: Persons committed as not criminally responsible on conditional release, individuals found incompetent to stand trial who require community monitoring, behavioral health and healthcare providers, defense attorneys and public defenders, and state prosecutors.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $97,000 in FY 2028 (reflecting the October 1, 2027 effective date for Section 1) to fund one part-time administrative employee and one part-time social worker within the Maryland Department of Health, increasing to $132,400 by FY 2032. The Office of the Public Defender may incur costs in future years if demand for social work representation increases. State revenues and local finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: SB 412 directly establishes and codifies the Community Forensic Aftercare Program within the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) and creates a community monitoring board to monitor individuals on conditional release, requiring MDH to hire additional personnel and adopt implementing regulations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes rapid record disclosure mandates to the Office of the Public Defender within 24 hours of request, permits public defender social workers or investigators to serve as authorized agents attending forensic review and monitoring meetings, and could result in future operational and staffing impacts.

The bill directly restricts court orders regarding clinical decisions for committed persons, governs court notices and hearing procedures for conditional release violations, and interfaces with judicial oversight of incompetent to stand trial (IST) and not criminally responsible (NCR) defendants.
The bill explicitly authorizes the Office of the Attorney General to provide legal counsel to the Department of Health at Community Forensic Aftercare Program community monitoring board meetings.

qa_results.bill_summary: Enacts the Maryland Worker Freedom Act, which prohibits employers from taking adverse action against employees or refusing to hire applicants who decline to attend employer-sponsored meetings or listen to communications conveying the employer's opinions on religious or political matters. It authorizes the Commissioner of Labor and Industry to investigate complaints, mediate disputes, assess civil penalties, and requires employers to post notices of employee rights.
qa_results.responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry (Maryland Department of Labor)
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland employers, employees, and job applicants
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $131,600 (specifically $131,588) in FY 2027 to hire 1.5 positions (one wage and hour investigator and a part-time assistant attorney general) to investigate complaints and enforce compliance, growing to $173,100 by FY 2031. Civil penalties of up to $10,000 for initial violations and $25,000 for subsequent violations are not anticipated to materially impact general fund revenues. State and local governments as employers are assumed to comply, resulting in no material expenditure impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary implementing and enforcement agency for the bill. The Commissioner of Labor and Industry is tasked with investigating complaints, conducting mediation, issuing penalties and relief orders, and developing and distributing workplace posters and model notices.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal representation and counsel to the Department of Labor. The fiscal note explicitly includes funding for a half-time Assistant Attorney General position to assist with enforcement, administrative proceedings, and court petitions.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Animal Research Modernization and Best Practices Act of 2026 prohibits research and testing facilities from performing devocalization surgery on dogs or cats or using devocalized dogs or cats for research or testing.
